drills.q: Fraud prevalence 0.1%. Model flags 5% of transactions, catches 80% of fraud. Compute precision.
drills.a: True positives = 0.8 x 0.001 = 0.0008; flagged = 0.05 -> precision = 0.0008/0.05 = 1.6%. Accuracy ~95%+ yet precision is terrible - exactly why accuracy is a vanity metric here.

drills.q: Selection rates: group A 45%, group B 30%. Adverse impact ratio and verdict under the four-fifths guideline?
drills.a: AIR = 0.30/0.45 = 0.667 < 0.80 -> fails the heuristic flag. Not legal proof by itself but triggers investigation: proxy features, threshold placement, segment-level decomposition before any remediation decision.

drills.q: Why can't you satisfy calibration-within-groups AND equal error rates when base rates differ?
drills.a: Mathematical impossibility (Kleinberg et al 2016; Chouldechova 2017): with differing base rates, equalizing FPR/FNR forces different positive-predictive values across groups, breaking calibration - and vice versa. Estimator quality changes magnitudes, never removes the tradeoff. Choose per context + document.

drills.q: A challenger credit GBM improves AUC +0.02 but drops the protected-group AIR from 0.91 to 0.77. Walk the governance path.
drills.a: Fairness guardrails are blocking metrics: no promotion. Quantify profit delta vs regulatory/litigation exposure, investigate driver (threshold vs feature), test mitigations (reweighting, feature removal) with re-audits, then escalate options memo to model governance + fair-lending compliance for a documented decision. Never ship silently.

drills.q: Your bank's credit-scoring system serves EU customers. Which EU AI Act date changes your roadmap and what must exist by then?
drills.a: Aug 2, 2026: Annex III high-risk obligations bite - risk-management system, data governance, technical documentation, logging, transparency, human oversight, robustness, conformity assessment. Retrofit takes quarters, so inventory mapping + gap analysis start now; watch simplification proposals for schedule shifts.

drills.q: Generate adverse-action reasons from a GBM: pipeline steps?
drills.a: Per-applicant SHAP attributions -> map top attributions to legal-approved reason-code vocabulary ('insufficient length of credit history') -> rank by magnitude -> fill Reg B letter templates within 30 days. The mapping layer itself needs validation - wrong reason codes violate even when scores are correct.

drills.q: AML alert queue: 10k alerts/month at 94% FP rate. Where do ML models help first?
drills.a: Alert scoring/prioritization: rank queues so investigators clear true positives earlier (ranking metric, not calibration); entity resolution merges duplicate subjects; graph analytics surface networks invisible transaction-by-transaction. Capacity math stays human: SAR narratives and referrals remain analyst-owned.

drills.q: Fraud score distribution compressed toward the safe zone over 6 weeks while chargeback lag hides labels. Diagnose.
drills.a: Classic adversarial probing signature: adversary tested until boundary softened. Actions: switch evaluation to delayed-feedback-aware metrics, compare feature-drift attribution (boundary-concentrated shift = hostile), rotate champion/retrain on recent confirmed patterns, add rules for observed new patterns, verify kill-switch to rules-only mode works.

drills.q: A lender wants to use alternative data (utility/rent payments, cash-flow history) to extend credit to thin-file applicants. What fair-lending risk does this introduce, and does improving aggregate access resolve it?
drills.a: Alternative data sources can correlate with protected-class membership through geography, employment type, or banking-access patterns -- the same proxy-discrimination risk as traditional features. Improving aggregate access does not automatically resolve fair-lending risk: a model can improve access overall while still showing disparate impact on specific decision margins (who's approved vs still denied) or pricing/terms -- requires outcome-level disparate-impact testing across the full decision, not just the headline approval-rate.

drills.q: Design question: your CEO wants to ship a more accurate but genuinely less-explainable deep learning underwriting model over an interpretable alternative. How do you handle it, and how does this shape your architecture choices from the start?
drills.a: Treat the adverse-action-reason-code requirement as a hard architectural constraint decided at model-selection time, not a bolt-on: use an interpretable-by-design model, or if a more complex model is justified by material accuracy gain, build and validate a stability-tested explanation pipeline BEFORE it generates real adverse decisions. Quantify the accuracy gain (reduced default losses) against the specific legal exposure (CFPB Circular 2026-03: complexity doesn't excuse compliance) -- invest in the explanation infrastructure up front rather than shipping first and fixing explainability later, since remediating live legally-deficient adverse-action notices (including liability for past decisions) is far more expensive.
